# The classical algebra of a window {#sec-classical-algebra}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="In this lecture"}
- We write the sine-Gordon equation as the flatness of a connection that depends on a spectral parameter $\lambda$, and find that $\lambda$ is a rapidity in disguise.
- Bäcklund's transformation is a gauge transformation of this connection, by a matrix linear in $1/\lambda$. This is why Bäcklund's machine works.
- Freezing the gauge transformation at a point finds the window a third time, after Bäcklund's machine in Lecture 2 and momentum in Lecture 3. Only the two types of Lecture 3 survive.
- The window's matrix knows the window. Its eigenvalues on the vacuum give the delay of Lecture 4, and its determinant vanishes at the defect rapidity.
- A conserved generating function gives all the charges. We compute those of spin $\mp1$ and $\mp3$ with their window terms, and find that a jump of $2\pi$ stores the higher charges of a soliton too.
- The kinetic term that momentum fixed is exactly the Poisson bracket that makes the window's matrix a classical L-operator for the bulk r-matrix. So the charges are in involution.

*Prerequisites:* @sec-backlund-machine, in particular @sec-l2-machine and @sec-l2-bianchi; @sec-freezing, in particular @sec-l3-lagrangian, @sec-l3-sine-gordon and @sec-l3-rapidity; @sec-what-gets-through, in particular @sec-l4-delay and @sec-l4-waves. From the book: the [Lax pair](book:sec-lax-pair), its [conserved charges](book:sec-conserved-charges) and [Sklyanin's formalism](book:sec-sklyanin).
:::

## The question {#sec-l6-question}

Lecture 3 found the window from a single requirement, the conservation of a modified momentum. It ended by asking whether momentum is enough (@sec-l3-enough). Integrability needs infinitely many conserved charges, and they must Poisson-commute. Checking them one at a time is hopeless. The tool that produces all of them at once is a Lax pair. It writes the field equation as the flatness of a connection, and the parallel transport of a flat connection around a circle gives a conserved generating function. A window cuts the circle at $x=0$. Something must carry the transport across the cut, and that something must have the right Poisson brackets. This lecture asks:

> Why are the windows integrable, in the language of Lax pairs and r-matrices?

Two things must be shown. The window must have a matrix that lets the transport cross it, so that the generating function survives. And that matrix must have the right Poisson brackets, so that the charges commute. Both turn out to be things we already know, in disguise.

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict"}
At a mirror, the transport is reflected by a matrix $K$ that does not depend on the fields (see the book's [Sklyanin formalism](book:prp-sklyanin)). Should the window's matrix depend on the values of the fields at $x=0$? On the spectral parameter $\lambda$, which we will find to be a rapidity? What should happen to the matrix at the defect rapidity $\theta_d$, where Lecture 4 found that a soliton is absorbed?
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Where it comes from"}
In 1968 Lax wrote the Korteweg–de Vries equation as the compatibility condition of two linear problems [@lax1968]. In 1973 Ablowitz, Kaup, Newell and Segur did the same for the sine-Gordon equation, with a linear problem for vectors of two components, and solved it by inverse scattering [@akns1973]. The Hamiltonian side of the method, with its classical r-matrix, is told in the book of Faddeev and Takhtajan [@faddeev_takhtajan1987]. In 1988 Sklyanin showed how a boundary enters this machinery, through a matrix $K$ and a double-row transfer matrix [@sklyanin1988].

For windows, Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon built a Lax pair from two Lax pairs on overlapping regions, related by a gauge transformation in the overlap [@bcz2004, Sec. 4; @bcz2004b, Sec. 3]. In the affine Toda theories the construction appeared to work only for $a_r^{(1)}$, which Lecture 5 proved from momentum, under its assumptions. In 2007 Caudrelier took the route of inverse scattering [@caudrelier2008]. He built the generating function of all the modified charges, identified the window's contribution to all orders through a defect matrix, described windows as Bäcklund transformations localized at a point, and classified the possible defect matrices. The Poisson brackets proved delicate, because the defect matrix involves the fields at the point where the two halves meet. Habibullin and Kundu regularized the window on a lattice and found its classical and quantum R-matrices and all its charges [@habibullin_kundu2008]. Avan and Doikou based integrability on the r-matrix algebra, and found the conditions at the window from the continuity of the time components of the Lax pairs [@avan_doikou2012a; @avan_doikou2012b]. Caudrelier and Kundu, and then Caudrelier for sine-Gordon theory, introduced a second Poisson bracket, in which $x$ plays the role of time [@caudrelier_kundu2015; @caudrelier2015]. In it the defect conditions are a canonical transformation, and the problem of fields at coinciding points does not arise.
:::

## The Lax pair {#sec-l6-lax}

**Matrices.** We use the $2\times2$ matrices

$$
\mathsf h=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad
\mathsf e=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\mathsf f=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\mathsf s=\mathsf e+\mathsf f,\quad
\mathsf y=-i\mathsf e+i\mathsf f,
$$

with $[\mathsf h,\mathsf e]=2\mathsf e$, $[\mathsf h,\mathsf f]=-2\mathsf f$ and $[\mathsf e,\mathsf f]=\mathsf h$. The matrices $\mathsf s$, $\mathsf y$, $\mathsf h$ are Pauli's three matrices, but we keep the letter $\sigma$ for the defect parameter. They satisfy $\mathsf h^2=\mathsf s^2=\mathsf y^2=1$, $\mathsf{sy}=i\mathsf h$, $[\mathsf h,\mathsf s]=2i\mathsf y$ and $[\mathsf h,\mathsf y]=-2i\mathsf s$. Most calculations in this lecture rest on two rules. First, $\mathsf s$ anticommutes with $\mathsf h$, so $\mathsf s\,e^{i\alpha\mathsf h}=e^{-i\alpha\mathsf h}\mathsf s$ for every $\alpha$. Second, $e^{i\alpha\mathsf h}=\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha\,\mathsf h$, so $e^{i\alpha\mathsf h}-e^{-i\alpha\mathsf h}=2i\sin\alpha\,\mathsf h$. The field enters through

$$
\mathsf s_\Phi:=e^{i\Phi\mathsf h/4}\,\mathsf s\,e^{-i\Phi\mathsf h/4}=e^{i\Phi\mathsf h/2}\mathsf s=e^{i\Phi/2}\mathsf e+e^{-i\Phi/2}\mathsf f .
$$

It has $\mathsf s_0=\mathsf s$, $\mathsf s_{2\pi}=-\mathsf s$ and $\partial_\Phi\mathsf s_\Phi=\frac i4[\mathsf h,\mathsf s_\Phi]$. By the first rule $\mathsf s_\Phi\mathsf s_{-\Phi}=e^{i\Phi\mathsf h}$, so by the second $[\mathsf s_\Phi,\mathsf s_{-\Phi}]=2i\sin\Phi\,\mathsf h$.

**The pair.** With a complex spectral parameter $\lambda\ne0$ set

$$
\mathcal A_+=\frac i4\,\partial_+\Phi\,\mathsf h+\frac{m_0\lambda}2\,\mathsf s_\Phi,\qquad
\mathcal A_-=-\frac i4\,\partial_-\Phi\,\mathsf h-\frac{m_0}{2\lambda}\,\mathsf s_{-\Phi}.
$$ {#eq-l6-lax}

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\big[\partial_++\mathcal A_+,\partial_-+\mathcal A_-\big]&=\partial_+\mathcal A_--\partial_-\mathcal A_++[\mathcal A_+,\mathcal A_-]\\
&=-\frac i2\big(\partial_+\partial_-\Phi+m_0^2\sin\Phi\big)\,\mathsf h .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-l6-curvature}

So the connection is flat for every $\lambda$ exactly when $\Phi$ solves the sine-Gordon equation (-@eq-l2-sg). Here is the calculation, power by power in $\lambda$. By the chain rule $\partial_\pm\mathsf s_\Phi=\frac i4\partial_\pm\Phi\,[\mathsf h,\mathsf s_\Phi]$.

- At order $\lambda$: $-\partial_-\mathcal A_+$ contributes $-\frac{m_0\lambda}2\cdot\frac i4\partial_-\Phi\,[\mathsf h,\mathsf s_\Phi]$, and the commutator contributes $\frac{m_0\lambda}2\cdot\big(-\frac i4\partial_-\Phi\big)[\mathsf s_\Phi,\mathsf h]$, which is the same with the opposite sign.
- At order $1/\lambda$ the two terms cancel in the same way.
- At order $\lambda^0$: $-\frac i4\partial_+\partial_-\Phi\,\mathsf h-\frac i4\partial_-\partial_+\Phi\,\mathsf h-\frac{m_0^2}4[\mathsf s_\Phi,\mathsf s_{-\Phi}]=-\frac i2\partial_+\partial_-\Phi\,\mathsf h-\frac i2m_0^2\sin\Phi\,\mathsf h$.

**Space and time.** With $a_t=\frac12(\mathcal A_++\mathcal A_-)$ and $a_x=\frac12(\mathcal A_+-\mathcal A_-)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_t&=\frac i4\Phi_x\,\mathsf h+\frac{m_0}4\big(\lambda\,\mathsf s_\Phi-\lambda^{-1}\mathsf s_{-\Phi}\big),\\
a_x&=\frac i4\Phi_t\,\mathsf h+\frac{m_0}4\big(\lambda\,\mathsf s_\Phi+\lambda^{-1}\mathsf s_{-\Phi}\big).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-l6-components}

Since $\partial_\pm=\partial_t\pm\partial_x$, $[\partial_++\mathcal A_+,\partial_-+\mathcal A_-]=2[\partial_x+a_x,\partial_t+a_t]$. So the **linear problem**

$$
(\partial_x+a_x)\chi=0,\qquad(\partial_t+a_t)\chi=0,
$$

for a vector $\chi(t,x;\lambda)\in\mathbb C^2$, has a solution for every initial vector exactly when $\Phi$ solves the sine-Gordon equation. It is the book's [Lax pair](book:eq-lax-pair) for $a_1^{(1)}$, continued to imaginary coupling, with $\vec H=\mathsf h/\sqrt2$, $\beta\vec\alpha_1\cdot\vec\phi\to i\Phi$ and the book's $m$ equal to $m_0/2$ (@exr-l6-flat).

**What $\lambda$ is.** Two observations. First, a boost that raises every rapidity by $\vartheta$ multiplies $\partial_+$ by $e^{-\vartheta}$ and $\partial_-$ by $e^{\vartheta}$, as in @sec-l2-once. In (-@eq-l6-lax) this is undone by $\lambda\to e^\vartheta\lambda$. Second, the vacuum. At $\Phi=0$ both $a_x=\frac{m_0}4(\lambda+\lambda^{-1})\mathsf s$ and $a_t=\frac{m_0}4(\lambda-\lambda^{-1})\mathsf s$ are multiples of $\mathsf s$, whose eigenvectors are $(1,\pm1)$ with eigenvalues $\pm1$. At $\lambda=-e^{-\theta}$, $a_x=-\frac{m_0}2\cosh\theta\,\mathsf s$ and $a_t=\frac{m_0}2\sinh\theta\,\mathsf s$, so

$$
\chi=c_+\,e^{m_0\xi/2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}+c_-\,e^{-m_0\xi/2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\xi=x\cosh\theta-t\sinh\theta .
$$

The ratio of its two components in the eigenbasis of $\mathsf s$ is $\frac{c_+}{c_-}e^{m_0\xi}$, the function $Y$ of a soliton of rapidity $\theta$ (-@eq-l2-soliton). So $\lambda=-e^{-\theta}$ labels the rapidity $\theta$, as the parameter $a=-e^{-\theta}$ of Bäcklund's transformation did in Lecture 2. The next section shows that this is not an analogy.

**Parallel transport.** Let $T(x,y;\lambda)$ be the matrix that carries a solution of the $x$-equation from $y$ to $x$: $\partial_xT(x,y)=-a_x(x)T(x,y)$ and $T(y,y)=1$. Flatness gives its time dependence,

$$
\partial_tT(x,y)=-a_t(x)\,T(x,y)+T(x,y)\,a_t(y).
$$ {#eq-l6-transport}

The proof takes two lines. Let $K=\partial_tT+a_t(x)T-Ta_t(y)$. Using $\partial_xa_t-\partial_ta_x+[a_x,a_t]=0$, which is flatness, one finds $\partial_xK=-a_xK$, and $K(y,y)=0$. So $K=0$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check it yourself"}
Items (a) and (b) of `code/lectures/defects_l6_lax.py` check (-@eq-l6-curvature) with sympy, the identification with the book's $a_1^{(1)}$ Lax pair, the compensation of a boost by $\lambda\to e^\vartheta\lambda$, and the solutions on the vacuum at $\lambda=-e^{-\theta}$.
:::

## Why Bäcklund's machine works {#sec-l6-gauge}

Lecture 2 found a surprise. Bäcklund's two first-order equations for one function $\Psi$ are consistent exactly when $\Phi$ solves the sine-Gordon equation, and then $\Psi$ solves it too (@sec-l2-machine). We found this by cross-differentiating. Here is the reason.

**Gauge transformations.** Let $G(t,x;\lambda)$ be an invertible matrix and $\chi_\Phi$ a solution of the linear problem of $\Phi$. Then $\chi=G^{-1}\chi_\Phi$ solves $(\partial_\pm+\mathcal A'_\pm)\chi=0$ with $\mathcal A'_\pm=G^{-1}\mathcal A_\pm G+G^{-1}\partial_\pm G$, and the curvature of $\mathcal A'$ is $G^{-1}$ times the curvature of $\mathcal A$ times $G$. Suppose that $\mathcal A'$ is the connection of a second field $\Psi$, that is,

$$
\partial_\pm G=G\,\mathcal A_\pm(\Psi)-\mathcal A_\pm(\Phi)\,G .
$$ {#eq-l6-gauge}

Then, by (-@eq-l6-curvature), $\Psi$ solves the sine-Gordon equation if and only if $\Phi$ does. A gauge transformation between the two connections is a machine that turns solutions into solutions.

::: {#thm-l6-gauge}
## Bäcklund's transformation is a gauge transformation
**[Theorem]** Let $\sigma\ne0$, $\Sigma=\Phi+\Psi$, $\Delta=\Phi-\Psi$, and

$$
L_d(\lambda)=e^{i\Delta\mathsf h/4}+\frac\sigma\lambda\,e^{-i\Sigma\mathsf h/4}\mathsf s
=\begin{pmatrix}e^{i\Delta/4}&\frac\sigma\lambda e^{-i\Sigma/4}\\[2pt]\frac\sigma\lambda e^{i\Sigma/4}&e^{-i\Delta/4}\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-l6-Ld}

At any point, the $\partial_+$ equation (-@eq-l6-gauge) for $G=L_d$ holds for all $\lambda$ if and only if $\partial_+\Delta=-2\sigma m_0\sin\frac\Sigma2$, and the $\partial_-$ equation holds for all $\lambda$ if and only if $\partial_-\Sigma=\frac{2m_0}\sigma\sin\frac\Delta2$. So $L_d$ is a gauge transformation, $\chi_\Phi=L_d\,\chi_\Psi$, exactly when $\Psi=\mathfrak B_{-\sigma}\Phi$ is Bäcklund's transformation (-@eq-l2-bt) with $a=-\sigma$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $\mathsf D=e^{i\Delta\mathsf h/4}$ and $\mathsf O=e^{-i\Sigma\mathsf h/4}\mathsf s$, so that $L_d=\mathsf D+\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf O$. Both are invertible. Then $\mathsf O\mathsf h=-\mathsf h\mathsf O$, $\partial_\pm\mathsf D=\frac i4\partial_\pm\Delta\,\mathsf h\mathsf D$ and $\partial_\pm\mathsf O=-\frac i4\partial_\pm\Sigma\,\mathsf h\mathsf O$. We need four identities:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf D\,\mathsf s_\Psi&=\mathsf s_\Phi\,\mathsf D,&\mathsf O\,\mathsf s_\Psi-\mathsf s_\Phi\,\mathsf O&=-2i\sin\tfrac\Sigma2\,\mathsf h\mathsf D,\\
\mathsf O\,\mathsf s_{-\Psi}&=\mathsf s_{-\Phi}\,\mathsf O,&\mathsf D\,\mathsf s_{-\Psi}-\mathsf s_{-\Phi}\,\mathsf D&=2i\sin\tfrac\Delta2\,\mathsf h\mathsf O .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-l6-identities}

To prove them, write $\mathsf s_\Phi=e^{i\Phi\mathsf h/2}\mathsf s$ and move every $\mathsf s$ to the right with the first rule. For the second identity, $\mathsf O\mathsf s_\Psi=e^{-i\Sigma\mathsf h/4}\mathsf s\,e^{i\Psi\mathsf h/2}\mathsf s=e^{-i(\Phi+3\Psi)\mathsf h/4}$ and $\mathsf s_\Phi\mathsf O=e^{i\Phi\mathsf h/2}\mathsf s\,e^{-i\Sigma\mathsf h/4}\mathsf s=e^{i(3\Phi+\Psi)\mathsf h/4}$. Their difference is $\mathsf D\big(e^{-i\Sigma\mathsf h/2}-e^{i\Sigma\mathsf h/2}\big)=-2i\sin\frac\Sigma2\,\mathsf h\mathsf D$ by the second rule. The others are proved in the same way (@exr-l6-identities).

*The $\partial_+$ equation.* The right-hand side is $\big(\mathsf D+\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf O\big)\big(\frac i4\partial_+\Psi\,\mathsf h+\frac{m_0\lambda}2\mathsf s_\Psi\big)-\big(\frac i4\partial_+\Phi\,\mathsf h+\frac{m_0\lambda}2\mathsf s_\Phi\big)\big(\mathsf D+\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf O\big)$. Compare powers of $\lambda$.

- Order $\lambda$: $\frac{m_0}2(\mathsf D\mathsf s_\Psi-\mathsf s_\Phi\mathsf D)=0$, so there is nothing to match.
- Order $\lambda^0$: the right-hand side is $-\frac i4\partial_+\Delta\,\mathsf h\mathsf D+\frac{\sigma m_0}2(\mathsf O\mathsf s_\Psi-\mathsf s_\Phi\mathsf O)=-\frac i4\partial_+\Delta\,\mathsf h\mathsf D-i\sigma m_0\sin\frac\Sigma2\,\mathsf h\mathsf D$. The left-hand side is $\frac i4\partial_+\Delta\,\mathsf h\mathsf D$. They agree exactly when $\partial_+\Delta=-2\sigma m_0\sin\frac\Sigma2$.
- Order $\lambda^{-1}$: the right-hand side is $\frac{i\sigma}4\big(\partial_+\Psi\,\mathsf O\mathsf h-\partial_+\Phi\,\mathsf h\mathsf O\big)=-\frac{i\sigma}4\partial_+\Sigma\,\mathsf h\mathsf O$, which is $\sigma\partial_+\mathsf O$. This holds identically.

*The $\partial_-$ equation.* With $\mathcal A_-$ the roles of the orders are exchanged. Order $\lambda^0$ holds identically, because $\mathsf D$ commutes with $\mathsf h$. Order $\lambda^{-2}$ is $\mathsf O\mathsf s_{-\Psi}=\mathsf s_{-\Phi}\mathsf O$. Order $\lambda^{-1}$ reads $-\frac{i\sigma}4\partial_-\Sigma\,\mathsf h\mathsf O=\frac{i\sigma}4\partial_-\Sigma\,\mathsf h\mathsf O-\frac{m_0}2(\mathsf D\mathsf s_{-\Psi}-\mathsf s_{-\Phi}\mathsf D)=\frac{i\sigma}4\partial_-\Sigma\,\mathsf h\mathsf O-im_0\sin\frac\Delta2\,\mathsf h\mathsf O$, which holds exactly when $\partial_-\Sigma=\frac{2m_0}\sigma\sin\frac\Delta2$.
:::

The surprise of Lecture 2 is explained. The Bäcklund system is consistent because it says that $L_d$ intertwines two flat connections, and a gauge transformation maps flat connections to flat connections. The determinant is

$$
\det L_d=1-\frac{\sigma^2}{\lambda^2},
$$

so $L_d$ is invertible except at $\lambda=\pm\sigma$. Solutions of the linear problem cross from one field to the other as $\chi_\Psi=L_d^{-1}\chi_\Phi$. A Bäcklund transformation acts on the solutions of the linear problem by a matrix; such matrices are known as Darboux matrices [@rogers_schief2002].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check it yourself"}
Item (c) of `code/lectures/defects_l6_lax.py` checks with sympy that (-@eq-l6-gauge) holds for $L_d$ when the two Bäcklund equations hold, and that it fails for $1.3\sigma$. Item (e) checks $\det L_d$. Item (p) checks the identities (-@eq-l6-identities) and the four further identities of @sec-l6-frozen, with a wrong sign as a failing control.
:::

## Freezing the gauge transformation {#sec-l6-frozen}

At a window, $\Phi$ lives only on $x<0$ and $\Psi$ only on $x>0$. They meet at a single point, where only the time derivative of a matrix makes sense. Suppose that the solutions of the two linear problems are glued there by a matrix $G(t;\lambda)$, $\chi_\Phi(t,0)=G\,\chi_\Psi(t,0)$. Differentiate in time and use $\partial_t\chi=-a_t\chi$ on each side. The gluing is preserved for every $\chi_\Psi$ exactly when

$$
\partial_tG=G\,a_t(\Psi)-a_t(\Phi)\,G\qquad\text{at }x=0,
$$ {#eq-l6-time}

where $a_t(\Phi)$ contains $\Phi_x(t,0^-)$ and $a_t(\Psi)$ contains $\Psi_x(t,0^+)$. This is half the sum of the two equations (-@eq-l6-gauge). So $L_d$ glues the two linear problems whenever the defect conditions (-@eq-l4-conditions) hold. We now ask the question the other way round, as in Lecture 3, without assuming $L_d$.

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict"}
The matrix $L_d$ has the form $G_0+\lambda^{-1}G_1$. Which matrices of this form can satisfy (-@eq-l6-time) at a point, and what conditions on the fields do they impose? Expect a classification.
:::

**The extreme orders.** Insert $G=G_0+\lambda^{-1}G_1$, with matrices $G_0$ and $G_1$ that may depend on $t$, into (-@eq-l6-time), with $a_t$ from (-@eq-l6-components). Both sides are Laurent polynomials in $\lambda$, from $\lambda^1$ to $\lambda^{-2}$. At order $\lambda$ the equation is $G_0\mathsf s_\Psi=\mathsf s_\Phi G_0$. Write $G_0=e^{i\Phi\mathsf h/4}Me^{-i\Psi\mathsf h/4}$; the equation becomes $M\mathsf s=\mathsf sM$, so $M=p+q\,\mathsf s$ with two functions $p$, $q$ of $t$. At order $\lambda^{-2}$ the same argument applies to $G_1\mathsf s_{-\Psi}=\mathsf s_{-\Phi}G_1$. With $\bar{\mathsf O}:=e^{i\Sigma\mathsf h/4}\mathsf s=\mathsf s\,e^{-i\Sigma\mathsf h/4}$,

$$
G_0=p\,\mathsf D+q\,\bar{\mathsf O},\qquad G_1=p'\,\mathsf D^{-1}+q'\,\mathsf O .
$$

**The middle orders.** Besides (-@eq-l6-identities) we need two more identities of the same kind, $\mathsf D^{-1}\mathsf s_\Psi-\mathsf s_\Phi\mathsf D^{-1}=-2i\sin\frac\Delta2\,\mathsf h\bar{\mathsf O}$ and $\bar{\mathsf O}\mathsf s_{-\Psi}-\mathsf s_{-\Phi}\bar{\mathsf O}=2i\sin\frac\Sigma2\,\mathsf h\mathsf D^{-1}$, and the facts $\bar{\mathsf O}\mathsf h=-\mathsf h\bar{\mathsf O}$ and $\partial_t\bar{\mathsf O}=\frac i4\Sigma_t\,\mathsf h\bar{\mathsf O}$. The order $\lambda^0$ of (-@eq-l6-time) is then

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\dot p\,\mathsf D+\dot q\,\bar{\mathsf O}+\frac i4\big(p\,\Delta_t\,\mathsf h\mathsf D+q\,\Sigma_t\,\mathsf h\bar{\mathsf O}\big)\\
&\qquad=-\frac i4\big(p\,\Delta_x\,\mathsf h\mathsf D+q\,\Sigma_x\,\mathsf h\bar{\mathsf O}\big)-\frac{im_0}2\Big(q'\sin\frac\Sigma2\,\mathsf h\mathsf D+p'\sin\frac\Delta2\,\mathsf h\bar{\mathsf O}\Big).
\end{aligned}
$$

The matrices $\mathsf D$ and $\mathsf h\mathsf D$ are diagonal and $\bar{\mathsf O}$ and $\mathsf h\bar{\mathsf O}$ are off-diagonal, and each pair is linearly independent. So the four coefficients vanish separately: $\dot p=\dot q=0$, and, with $\Delta_t+\Delta_x=\partial_+\Delta$ and $\Sigma_t+\Sigma_x=\partial_+\Sigma$, the first and third equations below. The order $\lambda^{-1}$ gives $\dot p'=\dot q'=0$ and the other two in the same way (@exr-l6-identities):

$$
\begin{aligned}
p\,\partial_+\Delta&=-2m_0\,q'\sin\frac\Sigma2,&\qquad q'\,\partial_-\Sigma&=2m_0\,p\,\sin\frac\Delta2,\\
q\,\partial_+\Sigma&=-2m_0\,p'\sin\frac\Delta2,&\qquad p'\,\partial_-\Delta&=2m_0\,q\,\sin\frac\Sigma2 .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-l6-four}

The middle orders of (-@eq-l6-time) are equivalent to these four equations with constant $p$, $q$, $p'$, $q'$.

**Pairing.** As in Lecture 3, the defect values and the velocities $\Phi_t$, $\Psi_t$ can be chosen freely at any one instant, and the conditions at $x=0$ then determine $\Phi_x$ and $\Psi_x$. The first row of (-@eq-l6-four) pairs $p$ with $q'$. If one of the two is zero and the other is not, one equation reads $0={}$constant$\,\times\sin\frac\Sigma2$ or $0={}$constant$\,\times\sin\frac\Delta2$, a relation among the defect values, which is not allowed. So $p$ and $q'$ are both zero or both nonzero. The second row pairs $q$ with $p'$ in the same way. If all four constants are nonzero, the four equations fix $\partial_\pm\Delta$ and $\partial_\pm\Sigma$, that is all four first derivatives, as functions of the defect values; then the velocities are not free. And if all four vanish, $G=0$. One pair survives.

::: {#thm-l6-frozen}
## The window is the frozen gauge transformation
**[Theorem]** Let $G(t;\lambda)=G_0(t)+\lambda^{-1}G_1(t)$ be nonzero, and suppose that (-@eq-l6-time) holds for all $\lambda$, on a family of solutions in which the defect values and the velocities $\Phi_t(t,0)$, $\Psi_t(t,0)$ can take arbitrary values at any one instant. Then, up to a constant factor, either

- $G=L_d$ of (-@eq-l6-Ld), with $\sigma=q'/p$, and the fields obey the type-I$_-$ conditions (-@eq-l4-conditions); or
- $G=L_d^+:=\mathsf s\,e^{-i\Sigma\mathsf h/4}+\frac\sigma\lambda e^{-i\Delta\mathsf h/4}$, with $\sigma=p'/q$, and the fields obey the type-I$_+$ conditions $\partial_+\Sigma=-2\sigma m_0\sin\frac\Delta2$, $\partial_-\Delta=\frac{2m_0}\sigma\sin\frac\Sigma2$.

Conversely, $L_d$ and $L_d^+$ satisfy (-@eq-l6-time) on these conditions.
:::

::: {.proof}
The extreme orders give the forms of $G_0$ and $G_1$, and the middle orders give constant $p,q,p',q'$ and (-@eq-l6-four). By the pairing argument either $q=p'=0\ne p,q'$ or $p=q'=0\ne q,p'$. In the first case $G=p\big(\mathsf D+\frac{q'}{p\lambda}\mathsf O\big)=pL_d$, and the two surviving equations of (-@eq-l6-four) are the type-I$_-$ conditions with $\sigma=q'/p$. In the second case $G=q\big(\bar{\mathsf O}+\frac{p'}{q\lambda}\mathsf D^{-1}\big)=qL_d^+$, and the surviving equations are the type-I$_+$ conditions. The converse is the computation read backwards, or, for $L_d$, the time component of @thm-l6-gauge.
:::

The type-I$_+$ conditions are the type-I$_-$ conditions with $\Psi\to-\Psi$, which exchanges $\Sigma$ and $\Delta$, as in @sec-l3-types. In matrix language, $\mathcal A_\pm(-\Psi)=\mathsf s\,\mathcal A_\pm(\Psi)\,\mathsf s$ and $L_d^+=L_d(\Phi,-\Psi)\,\mathsf s$ (@exr-l6-types). The Lax pair has found the window a third time. Lecture 2 built it from Bäcklund's machine, Lecture 3 from momentum, and now the gluing of two linear problems at a point leaves the same two types, and nothing else of this form.

**Reading the matrix.** In $L_d$ the diagonal carries the jump $\Delta$, and the off-diagonal carries $\Sigma$ with the factor $\sigma$. These are the two halves of the defect potential (-@eq-l3-potential): the half with $\sigma^{-1}$ depends on $\Delta$, the half with $\sigma$ on $\Sigma$. By $\mathsf D\mathsf s_{-\Phi}=e^{-i\Sigma\mathsf h/4}\mathsf s$,

$$
L_d(\lambda)=e^{i\Delta\mathsf h/4}\Big(1+\frac\sigma\lambda\,\mathsf s_{-\Phi}\Big),
$$

which is the book's [defect matrix](book:eq-defect-lax-matrix) for $a_1^{(1)}$. Two further facts will matter.

- $L_d$ depends on $\lambda$ and $\sigma$ only through $\sigma/\lambda$. At $\lambda=-e^{-\theta}$ this is $-e^{\theta-\theta_d}$, a function of the rapidity relative to the window, as Lecture 4 found for everything a window does.
- At $\lambda=-\sigma$, which is $\theta=\theta_d$, $L_d=\mathsf D-\mathsf O$ has rank 1. Its kernel is spanned by $(1,e^{i\Phi/2})$, which involves only the left field.

The inverse of Bäcklund's transformation is $\mathfrak B_{-a}=\mathfrak B_a^{-1}$, by @exr-l2-inverse. In matrix language this is $L_d(\lambda;\sigma)(\Phi,\Psi)\,L_d(\lambda;-\sigma)(\Psi,\Phi)=\det L_d$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check it yourself"}
Item (d) of `code/lectures/defects_l6_lax.py` solves the order-$\lambda$ and order-$\lambda^{-2}$ equations for a general $2\times2$ matrix and finds exactly the forms of $G_0$ and $G_1$. It checks that the eight middle coefficients are an invertible combination of (-@eq-l6-four) and the four time derivatives, and that the four equations have rank 4 when all constants are nonzero. It recovers the two types. Item (e) checks the rank of $L_d(-\sigma)$ and its kernel. Item (n) checks $L_d^+$ on its conditions and the inverse. Item (p) checks $\mathcal A_\pm(-\Psi)=\mathsf s\mathcal A_\pm(\Psi)\mathsf s$, $L_d^+=L_d(\Phi,-\Psi)\mathsf s$ and the book's form of $L_d$.
:::

## What the matrix knows {#sec-l6-knows}

On the vacuum $\Phi=\Psi=0$ the defect matrix is $L_d=1+\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf s$. Its eigenvectors are the eigenvectors $(1,\pm1)$ of $\mathsf s$, with eigenvalues $1\pm\sigma/\lambda$.

**The delay.** At the soliton's value $\lambda=-e^{-\theta}$, with $\sigma=e^{-\theta_d}$, the ratio of the two eigenvalues is

$$
\frac{1-\sigma/\lambda}{1+\sigma/\lambda}=\frac{1+e^{\theta-\theta_d}}{1-e^{\theta-\theta_d}}=-\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2=z(\theta),
$$

the delay (-@eq-l4-delay) of a soliton that crosses the window. At $\lambda=ie^{-\theta}$ the same ratio is $\frac{1+ie^{\theta-\theta_d}}{1-ie^{\theta-\theta_d}}$, the transmission factor $\mathbb T(\theta)$ (-@eq-l4-T) of linear waves, with modulus 1.

**Why the delay.** Here is a heuristic reason, not a proof. In @sec-l6-lax we saw that the soliton's $Y$ is the ratio of the components of a vacuum solution $\chi$ along $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$, at $\lambda=-e^{-\theta}$. Across the window, $\chi_\Psi=L_d^{-1}\chi_\Phi$ divides these two components by the eigenvalues $1+\sigma/\lambda$ and $1-\sigma/\lambda$. Their ratio is multiplied by $z$, and so $Y\to zY$. A proof goes through the soliton's bound state of the linear problem and its norming constant (@exr-l6-norming).

**The determinant.** $\det L_d=1-\sigma^2/\lambda^2$ vanishes at $\lambda=\pm\sigma$, that is at $\theta=\theta_d$ and at $\theta=\theta_d+i\pi$. At $\theta=\theta_d$ the delay has its pole: a soliton is absorbed, as in @sec-l4-absorption. The window's matrix fails to be invertible exactly at the defect rapidity.

So the answers to the Predict box are: the window's matrix depends on the fields, unlike a mirror's $K$, because it is a gauge transformation between two different fields; it depends on $\lambda$ through $\sigma/\lambda$ alone, that is on the relative rapidity; and at $\theta=\theta_d$ it degenerates.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check it yourself"}
Item (e) of `code/lectures/defects_l6_lax.py` checks the vacuum eigenvalues, the delay and the transmission factor. Item (n) checks the matrices $L_d=1\pm\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf s$ on the even vacua $(0,0)$ and $(2\pi,2\pi)$, which @exr-l6-norming needs.
:::

## A conserved generating function {#sec-l6-monodromy}

**On a circle.** Put $\Phi$ on $[-\ell,0]$ and $\Psi$ on $[0,\ell]$, and identify $x=-\ell$ with $x=\ell$, so that the fields form a circle with a window at $x=0$. At the identified point the fields join smoothly: $\Psi(t,\ell)=\Phi(t,-\ell)$ and $\Psi_x(t,\ell)=\Phi_x(t,-\ell)$, with no winding. Transport a solution of the linear problem once around the circle, starting at $x=-\ell$: along $\Phi$ to $0$, across the window by $L_d^{-1}$, along $\Psi$ to $\ell$. This gives the **defect monodromy**

$$
\mathcal T_d(\lambda)=T^\Psi(\ell,0;\lambda)\,L_d(\lambda)^{-1}\,T^\Phi(0,-\ell;\lambda),\qquad\tau_d(\lambda)=\operatorname{tr}\mathcal T_d(\lambda).
$$ {#eq-l6-monodromy}

::: {#thm-l6-monodromy}
## The generating function
**[Theorem]** If $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ solve the sine-Gordon equation on their intervals, join smoothly at $x=\pm\ell$ and obey the type-I$_-$ conditions at $x=0$, then $\tau_d(\lambda)$ is independent of $t$ for every $\lambda\ne\pm\sigma$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By (-@eq-l6-time), $\partial_tL_d^{-1}=-L_d^{-1}(\partial_tL_d)L_d^{-1}=L_d^{-1}a_t(\Phi)-a_t(\Psi)L_d^{-1}$ at $x=0$. With (-@eq-l6-transport) for both transport matrices, the terms at $x=0$ cancel in pairs:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\partial_t\mathcal T_d={}&\big[-a_t(\Psi;\ell)T^\Psi+T^\Psi a_t(\Psi;0)\big]L_d^{-1}T^\Phi+T^\Psi\big[L_d^{-1}a_t(\Phi;0)-a_t(\Psi;0)L_d^{-1}\big]T^\Phi\\
&+T^\Psi L_d^{-1}\big[-a_t(\Phi;0)T^\Phi+T^\Phi a_t(\Phi;-\ell)\big]
=-a_t(\Psi;\ell)\,\mathcal T_d+\mathcal T_d\,a_t(\Phi;-\ell).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the fields join smoothly, $a_t(\Psi;\ell)=a_t(\Phi;-\ell)$, so $\partial_t\mathcal T_d$ is a commutator and its trace vanishes.
:::

The window enters the generating function through one matrix, $L_d^{-1}$, which depends only on the defect values. Every coefficient of the expansion of $\tau_d$ in $\lambda$ is a conserved charge, and its window term is a function of the defect values and their derivatives. We expand it in @sec-l6-charges.

**On the line.** On the whole line the fields tend to vacua $2\pi n$, and the transport over a long interval grows exponentially. In the gauge $\chi=e^{i\Phi\mathsf h/4}\tilde\chi$ every vacuum has the same connection, $\tilde a_x=k\,\mathsf s$ with $k=\frac{m_0}4(\lambda+\lambda^{-1})$ and $\tilde a_t=\frac{m_0}4(\lambda-\lambda^{-1})\mathsf s$, because $\mathsf s_{4\pi n}=\mathsf s$. The window becomes $\tilde L_d=e^{-i\Phi\mathsf h/4}L_de^{i\Psi\mathsf h/4}=1+\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf s_{-\Sigma}$. The regularized monodromy $e^{k\mathsf sx_+}\tilde T(x_+,0)\tilde L_d^{-1}\tilde T(0,x_-)e^{-k\mathsf sx_-}$, with $x_\pm\to\pm\infty$, then has constant diagonal entries in the eigenbasis of $\mathsf s$. We do not prove this here; the script checks it numerically along an exact passage of a soliton, for real and complex $\lambda$, and finds that it fails without the window's matrix or with a wrong $\sigma$.

@fig-l6-holonomy shows the same thing in its simplest form. Flatness means that parallel transport around a closed loop is the identity. With a window inside the loop, this holds exactly when the loop crosses the window with $L_d$.

![Parallel transport around a window. (a) The exact passage of a soliton with $\theta=0.6$ through a window with $\theta_d=1$ ($m_0=1$), shown by its charge density $\partial_x\Phi$ on both sides; the dotted line is the world line the soliton would have without the window. The rectangle from $t_1$ to $t_2$ between $x=-6$ and $x=6$ crosses the window, with $L_d^{-1}$ at $t_1$ and $L_d$ at $t_2$. (b) The deviation $\Vert H-1\Vert$ of the holonomy $H$ around the rectangle from the identity, for $\lambda=0.8+0.5i$, against $t_2$. With $L_d$ it stays at the level of the numerical error, about $10^{-11}$. With $L_d$ replaced by 1, or with $\sigma$ replaced by $1.3\sigma$, it is of order 0.1 to 30. A flat connection with a seam has holonomy 1 only if the seam is crossed with the right matrix. `code/lectures/defects_l6_f1_holonomy.py` checks that the pair satisfies the defect conditions, that the holonomy is 1 to $10^{-9}$ with $L_d$, and that it deviates by more than 0.1 in the two controls.](figures/l6_holonomy.svg){#fig-l6-holonomy fig-alt="Left: a space-time density plot with a dark diagonal band, the soliton, crossing a vertical line at x equals zero, and a grey rectangle with arrows around it that crosses the line at two marked points labelled L_d inverse and L_d. Right: three curves on a logarithmic scale against t_2. A purple curve stays near ten to the minus eleven; an orange curve and a dashed teal curve lie between ten to the minus one and ten squared."}

**Windows and mirrors.** A mirror's generating function is Sklyanin's double row (see the book's [double-row transfer matrix](book:eq-double-row)). It contains $T(\lambda)$ and $T(1/\lambda)$ together, so its expansions at $\lambda\to\infty$ and $\lambda\to0$ are the same, and only the combinations $Q_s+Q_{-s}$ survive. The window's generating function contains a single $\lambda$, and its two ends are independent. So $Q_s$ and $Q_{-s}$ survive separately, each with its own window term. This is the classical form of the statement in @sec-l1-momentum.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check it yourself"}
Item (f) of `code/lectures/defects_l6_lax.py` computes the regularized monodromy along the passage $\Phi=4\arctan Y$, $\Psi=4\arctan(zY)$, in the gauge above, for real and complex $\lambda$. Its diagonal entries are constant to $10^{-8}$ and change by more than $10^{-2}$ with $L_d\to1$ or $\sigma\to1.3\sigma$. Item (e) checks the gauge form $\tilde L_d$.
:::

## The charges {#sec-l6-charges}

The window terms of all the charges sit in one place, the factor $L_d^{-1}$ of (-@eq-l6-monodromy). We extract the first few. From now on we write $\beta$ for $\beta_{\rm SG}$, so that the conserved quantities of Lecture 3 are $E\mp P+(\mathcal B\mp P_d)/\beta^2$.

**Step 1: a gauge in which the vacuum is diagonal.** As on the line, use $\chi=e^{i\Phi\mathsf h/4}\tilde\chi$. Then $\tilde a_x=\frac i4\partial_+\Phi\,\mathsf h+\frac{m_0\lambda}4\mathsf s+\frac{m_0}{4\lambda}\mathsf s_{-2\Phi}$, since $\Phi_t+\Phi_x=\partial_+\Phi$. Rotate by the Hadamard matrix $\mathsf u=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, which has $\mathsf{usu}=\mathsf h$, $\mathsf{uhu}=\mathsf s$ and $\mathsf{uyu}=-\mathsf y$. With $\mathsf s_\alpha=\cos\frac\alpha2\,\mathsf s-\sin\frac\alpha2\,\mathsf y$,

$$
\hat a=\frac{m_0\lambda}4\mathsf h+\frac i4\partial_+\Phi\,\mathsf s+\frac{m_0}{4\lambda}\big(\cos\Phi\,\mathsf h-\sin\Phi\,\mathsf y\big),\qquad
\hat L_d=1+\frac\sigma\lambda\Big(\cos\frac\Sigma2\,\mathsf h-\sin\frac\Sigma2\,\mathsf y\Big).
$$

The trace of the monodromy is unchanged, because the gauge matrix $e^{i\Phi\mathsf h/4}\mathsf u$ takes the same value at the two ends of the circle.

**Step 2: diagonalize the transport.** For large $\lambda$ the leading term $\frac{m_0\lambda}4\mathsf h$ dominates. Write the transport as $\hat T(x,y)=\big(1+W(x)\big)e^{Z(x,y)}\big(1+W(y)\big)^{-1}$, with $W$ off-diagonal and $Z$ diagonal. Insert this into $\partial_x\hat T=-\hat a\hat T$ and separate the diagonal and the off-diagonal parts. With $\hat a_{\rm d}$ and $\hat a_{\rm o}$ the diagonal and off-diagonal parts of $\hat a$,

$$
Z'=-\hat a_{\rm d}-\big(\hat a_{\rm o}W\big)_{\rm d},\qquad
W'=-\hat a_{\rm o}-\big[\hat a_{\rm d},W\big]+W\hat a_{\rm o}W ,
$$ {#eq-l6-riccati}

where the prime is $\partial_x$. The second equation is a matrix Riccati equation. Solve it as a series $W=\sum_{n\ge1}W_n\lambda^{-n}$. The commutator $[\mathsf h,W_{n+1}]$ appears at each order with the factor $\frac{m_0}4$, and it is invertible on off-diagonal matrices: $[\mathsf h,\alpha\mathsf s+\gamma\mathsf y]=2i\alpha\mathsf y-2i\gamma\mathsf s$. At order $\lambda^0$, $0=-\frac i4\partial_+\Phi\,\mathsf s-\frac{m_0}4[\mathsf h,W_1]$, so

$$
W_1=\frac{\partial_+\Phi}{2m_0}\,\mathsf y .
$$

**Step 3: the density.** The $2,2$ entry of $Z'$ dominates for large positive $\lambda$, since $\hat a_{22}=-\frac{m_0\lambda}4$. Its order $\lambda^{-1}$ has two parts: $\frac{m_0}4\cos\Phi$ from $-\hat a_{\rm d}$, and $-\frac{(\partial_+\Phi)^2}{8m_0}$ from $-(\hat a_{\rm o}W_1)_{22}$, using $\mathsf{sy}=i\mathsf h$. So

$$
Z'_{22}=\frac{m_0\lambda}4+\frac1\lambda\Big[\frac{m_0}4-\frac1{4m_0}\Big(\frac12(\partial_+\Phi)^2+V(\Phi)\Big)\Big]+O(\lambda^{-2}).
$$

With $\frac12(\partial_+\Phi)^2=\frac12\Phi_t^2+\frac12\Phi_x^2+\Phi_t\Phi_x$, the integral of the bracket is $\beta^2$ times the energy minus the momentum.

**Step 4: the window.** In the trace, the factors $1+W$ at $x=\pm\ell$ cancel by cyclicity, and those at $x=0$ combine with the window into $N=\big(1+W^\Psi(0)\big)^{-1}\hat L_d^{-1}\big(1+W^\Phi(0)\big)$. For large positive $\lambda$ only the $2,2$ entries survive, up to exponentially small terms:

$$
\ln\tau_d=Z^\Phi_{22}(0,-\ell)+Z^\Psi_{22}(\ell,0)+\ln N_{22},\qquad\ln N_{22}=\frac\sigma\lambda\cos\frac\Sigma2+O(\lambda^{-2}),
$$

because $\hat L_d^{-1}=1-\frac\sigma\lambda(\cos\frac\Sigma2\,\mathsf h-\sin\frac\Sigma2\,\mathsf y)+O(\lambda^{-2})$ and $W$ is off-diagonal. With $\sigma\cos\frac\Sigma2=\sigma-\frac1{4m_0}(\mathcal B-P_d)$, from @sec-l3-rapidity,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln\tau_d(\lambda)={}&\frac{m_0\ell}2\lambda+\frac1\lambda\Big[\frac{m_0\ell}2+\sigma-\frac1{4m_0}\Big(\beta^2(E-P)+\mathcal B-P_d\Big)\Big]\\
&+O(\lambda^{-2}),\qquad\lambda\to+\infty .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-l6-spin1}

The coefficient of $\lambda^{-1}$ is conserved, so $E-P+(\mathcal B-P_d)/\beta^2$ is conserved. This is Lecture 3's result, now one coefficient of a generating function. The bulk density is $\frac12(\partial_+\Phi)^2+V$, of spin $-1$, and the window's share is the half of $\mathcal B$ that depends on $\Sigma$, with $\sigma$.

**At $\lambda\to0$.** The other end of the $\lambda$-plane works the same way with $\partial_-$ in place of $\partial_+$. Use the gauge $e^{-i\Phi\mathsf h/4}$, in which $a_x\to\frac i4\partial_-\Phi\,\mathsf h+\frac{m_0}{4\lambda}\mathsf s+\frac{m_0\lambda}4\mathsf s_{2\Phi}$ and $L_d\to e^{i\Delta\mathsf h/2}+\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf s$. After the rotation by $\mathsf u$ the window is $\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf h+\cos\frac\Delta2+i\sin\frac\Delta2\,\mathsf s$, and the logarithm of the dominant entry of its inverse is $\ln(-\lambda/\sigma)+\frac\lambda\sigma\cos\frac\Delta2+O(\lambda^2)$. So $E+P+(\mathcal B+P_d)/\beta^2$ is conserved too, with the window's share the half of $\mathcal B$ that depends on $\Delta$, with $\sigma^{-1}$ (@exr-l6-zero).

**Spin $\mp3$.** Carry the expansion two orders further. Then $W_2=\frac i{2m_0^2}\partial_+^2\Phi\,\mathsf s$, after using the field equation; the density at order $\lambda^{-2}$ vanishes; and at order $\lambda^{-3}$ the density is

$$
\frac1{8m_0^3}\,q_-(\Phi)-\partial_x\Big(\frac{\partial_+\Phi\,\partial_+^2\Phi}{4m_0^3}\Big),\qquad q_-(\Phi)=(\partial_+^2\Phi)^2-\frac14(\partial_+\Phi)^4+m_0^2\cos\Phi\,(\partial_+\Phi)^2 .
$$

The density $q_-$ is the book's [spin-3 density](book:eq-spin3-current), continued to sine-Gordon theory. The total derivative is not harmless here. Its integral over $[-\ell,0]$ and $[0,\ell]$ leaves terms at $x=0$ from both sides, which join the order $\lambda^{-3}$ of $\ln N_{22}$. These terms contain $\partial_+^2\Phi$ and $\partial_+^2\Psi$ at the window. The defect conditions remove them: $\partial_+\Psi=\partial_+\Phi+2\sigma m_0\sin\frac\Sigma2$, and $\partial_+^2\Delta=2\partial_t(\partial_+\Delta)-\partial_-\partial_+\Delta$ expresses the difference of the second derivatives through a time derivative of the first condition and the field equations. What is left depends only on the defect values and on $\partial_+\Phi$, $\partial_+\Psi$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal D_{-3}&=\frac\sigma{2m_0^2}\cos\frac\Sigma2\,\partial_+\Phi\,\partial_+\Psi+\sigma^3\Big(\cos\frac\Sigma2-\frac23\cos^3\frac\Sigma2\Big),\\
\mathcal D_{+3}&=-\frac1{2m_0^2\sigma}\cos\frac\Delta2\,\partial_-\Phi\,\partial_-\Psi+\sigma^{-3}\Big(\cos\frac\Delta2-\frac23\cos^3\frac\Delta2\Big),
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-l6-D3}

where $\mathcal D_{+3}$ comes from the order $\lambda^3$ at $\lambda\to0$, with $q_+$ the same as $q_-$ with $\partial_-$ in place of $\partial_+$. Note the minus sign in $\mathcal D_{+3}$. The conserved charges of spin $\mp3$ are

$$
Q_{\mp3}=\frac1{8m_0^3}\Big[\int_{-\ell}^0q_\mp(\Phi)\,dx+\int_0^\ell q_\mp(\Psi)\,dx\Big]+\mathcal D_{\mp3}.
$$

You can check $\mathcal D_{-3}$ without the expansion. The flux of $q_-$ into the window from the two sides must be $-\frac d{dt}\mathcal D_{-3}$ on the defect conditions (@exr-l6-spin3). Like the window terms of spin $\mp1$, $\mathcal D_{-3}$ contains only the half $\Sigma$ with $\sigma$, and $\mathcal D_{+3}$ only the half $\Delta$ with $\sigma^{-1}$. The expansion is formal, as in the book's [both spin-two charges survive](book:prp-spin-two); we present the window terms as the result of a calculation that the script checks, not as a theorem.

**A jump stores every charge.** A soliton of rapidity $\theta$ carries $\beta^2(E\mp P)=8m_0e^{\mp\theta}$ and $\frac1{8m_0^3}\int q_\mp\,dx=-\frac23e^{\mp3\theta}$ (@exr-l6-spin3). At the static odd jump $(\Phi,\Psi)=(0,2\pi)$, $\cos\frac\Sigma2=\cos\frac\Delta2=-1$. So $\mathcal D_{\mp3}=-\frac13\sigma^{\pm3}$ there, while the even vacuum $(0,0)$ has $\mathcal D_{\mp3}=\frac13\sigma^{\pm3}$. Relative to the even vacuum the jump stores $-\frac23\sigma^{\pm3}=-\frac23e^{\mp3\theta_d}$, which is the spin-$\mp3$ charge of a soliton of rapidity $\theta_d$. Lecture 3 found that a jump of $2\pi$ stores the energy and momentum of a soliton (@sec-l3-rapidity). It stores its higher charges as well. @fig-l6-charges follows the four charges through a passage in which the window holds a soliton for a while.

![The window holds every charge of a soliton. A soliton with $\theta=\theta_d-0.01$ crosses a window with $\theta_d=0.8$ ($m_0=1$). It is held by the window for about six time units (grey), the time $\ln|z|/(m_0\sinh\theta)$ of @sec-l4-reading. The four panels show the charges of spin $-1$, $+1$, $-3$ and $+3$, split into the share of the field on $x<0$, the share of the window and the share of the field on $x>0$, as fractions of the total, which is constant (dashed). The window terms are $\mathcal B\mp P_d$ and $\mathcal D_{\mp3}$ minus their values $\frac13\sigma^{\pm3}$ on the even vacuum. During the hold the window holds the whole of each charge. The shares of spin $\pm3$ leave the interval $[0,1]$, because their densities are not positive; only the sum is fixed. `code/lectures/defects_l6_f2_charges.py` checks the defect conditions, the constancy of each sum to $10^{-8}$, that the totals are the charges of a soliton of rapidity $\theta$, that each window term holds the total to within 5% half-way through the hold, and that the odd jump stores the charges of a soliton of rapidity $\theta_d$.](figures/l6_charges.svg){#fig-l6-charges fig-alt="Four panels of curves against time. In each, a blue curve falls from one to zero, a purple curve rises from zero to about one during a grey band and falls back, and a red curve rises from zero to one after the band; a dashed line stays at one. In the lower two panels the curves overshoot to about 1.2 and dip to about minus 0.2 near the transitions."}

Item (g) of `code/lectures/defects_l6_lax.py` runs the Riccati recursion (-@eq-l6-riccati) symbolically. It finds $W_1$, the densities of orders $\lambda^{-1}$ to $\lambda^{-3}$, the window terms $\sigma\cos\frac\Sigma2$ and $\mathcal D_{-3}$, and checks numerically that the totals of spin $-1$ and $-3$ are constant along an exact passage, and not without the window terms. Item (h) does the same at $\lambda\to0$, with $\mathcal D_{+3}$. ## The Poisson bracket of a window {#sec-l6-poisson}

A conserved generating function gives infinitely many charges. For integrability they must also Poisson-commute. This needs brackets: the bulk bracket, and a bracket for the two defect values.

**The bracket of the window.** Lecture 3 noticed that the defect term $L_d=\Phi\Psi_t-\mathcal B$ is the phase-space Lagrangian $p\dot q-H$ of one degree of freedom (@sec-l3-lagrangian). With the factor $1/\beta^2$ of the action, the coordinate is $q=\Psi(t,0)$ and the momentum is $p=\Phi(t,0)/\beta^2$. So $\{\Psi,\Phi/\beta^2\}=1$:

$$
\{\Phi,\Psi\}=-\beta^2\quad\text{(type I}_-),\qquad\{\Phi,\Psi\}=+\beta^2\quad\text{(type I}_+),
$$

the latter from the kinetic term $-\Phi\Psi_t$. The bulk bracket is $\{\Phi(x),\Phi_t(y)\}=\beta^2\delta(x-y)$, in the same convention. This is the book's [defect bracket](book:eq-dc-defect-bracket) for sine-Gordon theory.

**Notation.** For matrices $X$ and $Y$, $\{X\overset\otimes,Y\}$ is the $4\times4$ matrix with entries $\{X_{ij},Y_{kl}\}$, and $X_1=X\otimes1$, $Y_2=1\otimes Y$. Let $\Pi=\mathsf e\otimes\mathsf f+\mathsf f\otimes\mathsf e$.

::: {#prp-l6-bulk-r}
## The bulk r-matrix
**[Established]** [@faddeev_takhtajan1987] With the bulk bracket above,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\big\{a_x(\lambda_1;x)\overset\otimes,a_x(\lambda_2;y)\big\}&=\delta(x-y)\,\big[r(\lambda_1/\lambda_2),a_x(\lambda_1;x)\otimes1+1\otimes a_x(\lambda_2;y)\big],\\
r(z)&=-\frac{\beta^2}{16(z^2-1)}\Big[(z^2+1)\,\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h+4z\,\Pi\Big].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-l6-rmatrix}

The transport over an interval then satisfies $\{T(\lambda_1)\overset\otimes,T(\lambda_2)\}=-[r(\lambda_1/\lambda_2),T(\lambda_1)\otimes T(\lambda_2)]$. The matrix $r$ satisfies the classical Yang–Baxter equation, and it is the book's [r-matrix](book:prp-sklyanin) for $h=2$, with the book's $\beta^2$ replaced by $-\beta^2/2$.
:::

The sign of $\{T,T\}$ is the opposite of the sign in the bracket of $a_x$, because $T$ is generated by $-a_x$. The derivation of $r$ from the bracket of $a_x$ is a few lines (@exr-l6-rmatrix).

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict"}
The matrix $L_d$ is built from $e^{\pm i\Delta/4}$ and $e^{\pm i\Sigma/4}$. Its entries have constant brackets with each other up to factors, because $\{\Delta,\Sigma\}=2\{\Phi,\Psi\}$ is a constant. Can $\{L_d\overset\otimes,L_d\}$ have the Sklyanin form $[r,L_d\otimes L_d]$ with the bulk $r$? If so, what must $\{\Phi,\Psi\}$ be?
:::

::: {#thm-l6-sklyanin}
## The window is a classical L-operator
**[Theorem]** Give the defect values a constant bracket $\{\Phi,\Psi\}=c$, and look for an r-matrix of the form $r(z)=\alpha(z)\,\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h+\gamma(z)\,\Pi$ with

$$
\big\{L_d(\lambda_1)\overset\otimes,L_d(\lambda_2)\big\}=\Big[r\Big(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\Big),L_d(\lambda_1)\otimes L_d(\lambda_2)\Big].
$$ {#eq-l6-sklyanin}

It exists and is unique: $r(z)=\frac c{16(z^2-1)}\big[(z^2+1)\,\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h+4z\,\Pi\big]$. It is the bulk r-matrix (-@eq-l6-rmatrix) exactly when $c=-\beta^2$, the bracket of the type-I$_-$ kinetic term. Likewise $L_d^+$ satisfies (-@eq-l6-sklyanin) with the bulk $r$ exactly for the type-I$_+$ bracket $c=+\beta^2$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $L_d=\mathsf D+\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf O$ as in @thm-l6-gauge, and $\kappa=c/8$. Since $\{\Delta,\Sigma\}=2c$ and $\{\Delta,\Delta\}=\{\Sigma,\Sigma\}=0$, the chain rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\{\mathsf D_1,\mathsf O_2\}&=\tfrac i4\cdot\big(-\tfrac i4\big)\cdot2c\;\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h\,\mathsf D_1\mathsf O_2=\kappa\,\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h\,\mathsf D_1\mathsf O_2,\\
\{\mathsf O_1,\mathsf D_2\}&=-\kappa\,\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h\,\mathsf O_1\mathsf D_2,
\end{aligned}
$$

and $\{\mathsf D_1,\mathsf D_2\}=\{\mathsf O_1,\mathsf O_2\}=0$. With $X=\mathsf D_1\mathsf O_2$ and $X'=\mathsf O_1\mathsf D_2$,

$$
\{L_1,L_2\}=\kappa\sigma\,\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h\Big(\frac{X}{\lambda_2}-\frac{X'}{\lambda_1}\Big).
$$

On the other side, $r$ commutes with $\mathsf D_1\mathsf D_2$ and with $\mathsf O_1\mathsf O_2$: both $\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h$ and $\Pi$ commute with $\mathsf h\otimes1+1\otimes\mathsf h$ and with $\mathsf s\otimes\mathsf s$. So only the cross terms of $L_1L_2$ contribute. For these, $[\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h,X]=2\,\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h\,X$, because $\mathsf O$ anticommutes with $\mathsf h$ and $\mathsf D$ commutes with it, and $[\Pi,X]=-\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h\,X'$; the same holds with $X$ and $X'$ exchanged. (Check the last one with $\mathsf{ef}=\frac12(1+\mathsf h)$ and $\mathsf{fe}=\frac12(1-\mathsf h)$; @exr-l6-identities.) Hence

$$
[r,L_1L_2]=\sigma\,\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h\Big[\Big(\frac{2\alpha}{\lambda_2}-\frac\gamma{\lambda_1}\Big)X+\Big(\frac{2\alpha}{\lambda_1}-\frac\gamma{\lambda_2}\Big)X'\Big].
$$

The matrices $\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h\,X$ and $\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h\,X'$ are linearly independent. Matching their coefficients, with $z=\lambda_1/\lambda_2$, gives $2\alpha-\gamma/z=\kappa$ and $2\alpha-\gamma z=-\kappa$, whose unique solution is $\gamma=\frac{2\kappa z}{z^2-1}$, $\alpha=\frac{\kappa(z^2+1)}{2(z^2-1)}$. This is the stated $r$, and it equals (-@eq-l6-rmatrix) exactly when $\kappa=-\beta^2/8$. For type I$_+$, $L_d^+=L_d(\Phi,-\Psi)\,\mathsf s$, and $\{\Phi,-\Psi\}=-c$. The constant factor $\mathsf s$ on the right does no harm, because $\mathsf s\otimes\mathsf s$ commutes with $r$.
:::

This is the point of the lecture. Momentum fixed the kinetic term in Lecture 3, and with it the bracket $\{\Phi,\Psi\}=-\beta^2$. Momentum knows nothing about r-matrices. Yet the bracket it fixed is exactly the one for which the window's matrix is a classical L-operator for the bulk r-matrix. More is true. The window, by itself, determines the trigonometric r-matrix up to the factor $c$, and the bulk theory then fixes $c$. In Lecture 7 the same statement, after quantization, says that the window's transmission matrix is an L-operator for half of the quantum group.

**Involution.** From (-@eq-l6-sklyanin), $\{L_{d,1}^{-1},L_{d,2}^{-1}\}=L_{d,1}^{-1}L_{d,2}^{-1}\{L_{d,1},L_{d,2}\}L_{d,1}^{-1}L_{d,2}^{-1}=-[r,L_{d,1}^{-1}L_{d,2}^{-1}]$. This is the same quadratic algebra as that of $T$. If two matrices $X$ and $Y$ Poisson-commute and both satisfy $\{X_1,X_2\}=-[r,X_1X_2]$, then so does their product $XY$. So $\mathcal T_d$ of (-@eq-l6-monodromy) satisfies it, and

$$
\{\tau_d(\lambda_1),\tau_d(\lambda_2)\}=-\operatorname{tr}_{12}\big[r,\mathcal T_d(\lambda_1)\otimes\mathcal T_d(\lambda_2)\big]=0 .
$$

All the charges of @sec-l6-charges Poisson-commute. The same algebra holds for a product of several window matrices, each with its own canonical pair: their traces commute, which is the structure of a classical integrable lattice (@exr-l6-chain). We return to such chains of windows in Lecture 8.

**What this does not settle.** The argument treats the defect values as independent coordinates that Poisson-commute with the bulk fields. They are the endpoint values of the bulk fields, and the equal-time bracket of the field theory does not restrict to the values of the fields at a point in a well-defined way [@caudrelier2015, Sec. 1]. The book discusses the ways around this, the lattice regularization of Habibullin and Kundu, the algebraic approach of Avan and Doikou, and Caudrelier's second bracket, after its proposition on the [Poisson algebra of the defect matrix](book:prp-defect-involution). The next section describes the last of these.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check it yourself"}
Item (i) of `code/lectures/defects_l6_lax.py` derives $r$ from the canonical brackets, compares it with the book's, checks $r^{t_1t_2}(z)=-r(1/z)$ and the classical Yang–Baxter equation, and finds the sign of $\{T,T\}$ from a lattice transport. Item (j) checks the brackets of $\mathsf D$ and $\mathsf O$, the commutators of the proof, @thm-l6-sklyanin for both types, and that the wrong sign of $\{\Phi,\Psi\}$ fails. Item (k) checks the involution for chains of three windows, and that it fails if $L_d$ and $L_d^{-1}$ are mixed.
:::

## Space as time {#sec-l6-space-time}

Caudrelier's way out exchanges the roles of $x$ and $t$ [@caudrelier2015]. Consider the functional

$$
G[\Phi,\Psi]=\int dt\,\big(\Phi\Psi_t-\mathcal B(\Phi,\Psi)\big)
$$

of the defect values along the whole time axis. Its variational derivatives are $\delta G/\delta\Phi(0,t)=\Psi_t-\mathcal B_\Phi$ and $-\delta G/\delta\Psi(0,t)=\Phi_t+\mathcal B_\Psi$. By the defect conditions (-@eq-l3-conditions) these are $\Phi_x$ and $\Psi_x$. Now read $x$ as time. The momentum conjugate to $\Phi$ in this picture is $\partial\ell/\partial\Phi_x=-\Phi_x$. The two equations say that $-G$ is the generating function of a canonical transformation from $(\Phi,-\Phi_x)$ to $(\Psi,-\Psi_x)$ on the line $x=0$. The window is a canonical transformation in the time-like picture [@caudrelier2015, Prop. 3.1]. In the bracket of this picture, in which the fields along a line of constant $x$ are the coordinates, there is no problem with fields at coinciding points. Caudrelier showed that the sine-Gordon model is Hamiltonian in this bracket with the same r-matrix, and proved Liouville integrability with the window [@caudrelier2015, Sec. 3.3].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check it yourself"}
Item (m) of `code/lectures/defects_l6_lax.py` checks the two variational derivatives with sympy, and that they are the generating relations of the canonical transformation.
:::

## Two windows {#sec-l6-two-windows}

Two windows in a row give a field $\Phi_0$ on the left, a field $\Phi_1$ between them and $\Phi_{12}$ on the right. Bianchi's permutability theorem (@prp-l2-bianchi) says that the same $\Phi_{12}$ can be reached through a different middle field $\Phi_2$, by applying the two transformations in the other order. In matrix language, with $L(\sigma;\Phi,\Psi)$ for $L_d$ of (-@eq-l6-Ld),

$$
L(\sigma_1;\Phi_0,\Phi_1)\,L(\sigma_2;\Phi_1,\Phi_{12})=L(\sigma_2;\Phi_0,\Phi_2)\,L(\sigma_1;\Phi_2,\Phi_{12})\qquad\text{for all }\lambda,
$$

when $\Phi_{12}$ is given by Bianchi's formula (-@eq-l2-bianchi) with $a_k=-\sigma_k$. Both sides change sign together if $\Phi_{12}$ is moved to another branch. **Bianchi's square is a refactorization of two gauge matrices.** Two windows can be exchanged, if the field between them is changed. This is the classical counterpart of the relations between windows of Lecture 7. Refactorizations of this kind are classical in the theory of Darboux matrices; we have not traced their origin.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check it yourself"}
Item (l) of `code/lectures/defects_l6_lax.py` checks the refactorization at random values of the fields and of $\lambda$, and that it fails for a perturbed $\Phi_{12}$.
:::

## The window of $a_r^{(1)}$ {#sec-l6-ar}

Lecture 5 promised the Lax pair of its windows. In the components of @sec-l5-ar, with real coupling, $\phi_k$ summing to zero and indices modulo $h$, use the defining representation: $\vec H\cdot\vec v=\mathrm{diag}(v_0,\dots,v_r)$, $E_{\vec\alpha_j}=e_{j,j+1}$ and $E_{-\vec\alpha_j}=e_{j+1,j}$, where $e_{jk}$ is the matrix with a single 1 in row $j$ and column $k$. The book's [Lax pair](book:eq-lax-pair) becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal A_+&=\frac12\,\mathrm{diag}(\partial_+\phi_k)+m\lambda\sum_je^{(\phi_j-\phi_{j+1})/2}e_{j,j+1},\\
\mathcal A_-&=-\frac12\,\mathrm{diag}(\partial_-\phi_k)-\frac m\lambda\sum_je^{(\phi_j-\phi_{j+1})/2}e_{j+1,j}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Its curvature is diagonal, and its entries are minus the Toda equations (-@eq-l5-toda), by the same calculation as for (-@eq-l6-curvature). The window's matrix is

$$
(L_d)_{kk}=g_k^{1/2}=e^{(\phi_k-\psi_k)/2},\qquad(L_d)_{j+1,j}=\frac\sigma\lambda\,f_j^{1/2}=\frac\sigma\lambda\,e^{(\psi_j-\phi_{j+1})/2},
$$ {#eq-l6-ar-Ld}

with all other entries zero, and $f_j$, $g_j$ the halves of the defect potential (-@eq-l5-ar-potential). **The diagonal carries the half $g$ and the subdiagonal the half $f$**, as for sine-Gordon theory. On Lecture 5's light-cone conditions (-@eq-l5-ar-lightcone) the matrix satisfies both equations (-@eq-l6-gauge), so it glues the two linear problems at the window, and unfrozen it is the gauge transformation of the Bäcklund transformation of the Toda lattice. It is the book's [defect matrix](book:eq-defect-lax-matrix) $e^{\vec H\cdot(\vec\phi-\vec\psi)/2}\big[1+\frac\sigma\lambda\sum_je^{\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec w/2}E_{-\vec\alpha_j}\big]$, with $\vec w=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\phi-\mathsf E\vec\psi$, because $\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec w=\psi_j+\psi_{j+1}-2\phi_{j+1}$ (@exr-l6-types).

The generating function and the involution go through as for sine-Gordon theory. The book states the time equation of the defect matrix, with numerical checks (see its [defect Lax matrix](book:prp-defect-lax)). It checks the Sklyanin relation numerically for $a_1^{(1)}$ to $a_4^{(1)}$ (see its [Poisson algebra of the defect matrix](book:prp-defect-involution)), and shows that both spin-$\pm2$ charges survive, one at each end of the $\lambda$-plane (see its proposition that [both spin-two charges survive](book:prp-spin-two)).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check it yourself"}
Item (o) of `code/lectures/defects_l6_lax.py` checks the curvature of the $a_r^{(1)}$ pair symbolically for $h=3$, and the time equation of (-@eq-l6-ar-Ld) on Lecture 5's light-cone conditions for $h=2,\dots,5$ and complex $\lambda$; it fails for $1.2\sigma$. Item (r) checks both light-cone equations (-@eq-l6-gauge) separately, and the identity $\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec w=\psi_j+\psi_{j+1}-2\phi_{j+1}$.
:::

## What we have learned {#sec-l6-summary}

- The sine-Gordon equation is the flatness of the connection (-@eq-l6-lax) for every $\lambda$, and $\lambda=-e^{-\theta}$ is the rapidity of a soliton.
- Bäcklund's transformation is a gauge transformation of this connection, by the matrix $L_d=e^{i\Delta\mathsf h/4}+\frac\sigma\lambda e^{-i\Sigma\mathsf h/4}\mathsf s$. This is why it is consistent and maps solutions to solutions.
- Gluing the two linear problems at a point by a matrix linear in $1/\lambda$ is possible only for the two types of window of Lecture 3, with their defect conditions. The window is the frozen gauge transformation.
- On the vacuum the ratio of the eigenvalues of $L_d$ is the delay of a soliton and the transmission factor of a wave. $\det L_d$ vanishes at the defect rapidity.
- The trace of the monodromy with $L_d^{-1}$ at the window is conserved. Its expansions at $\lambda\to\infty$ and $\lambda\to0$ give the charges of the two chiralities separately, each with a local window term. A jump of $2\pi$ stores all the charges of a soliton of rapidity $\theta_d$.
- The kinetic term fixed by momentum gives $\{\Phi,\Psi\}=-\beta^2$, exactly the bracket for which $L_d$ is a classical L-operator for the bulk r-matrix. The window alone determines the r-matrix up to a factor. The charges are in involution, if the defect values are treated as independent of the bulk.

## Exercises {#sec-l6-exercises}

::: {#exr-l6-flat}
*(Redo.)* Derive (-@eq-l6-curvature) and the time dependence (-@eq-l6-transport) of the transport. Show that a boost that raises all rapidities by $\vartheta$ maps the connection of a solution at $\lambda$ to the connection of the boosted solution at $e^{-\vartheta}\lambda$. Then write out the book's [Lax pair](book:eq-lax-pair) for $a_1^{(1)}$, with $\vec\alpha_1=-\vec\alpha_0=\sqrt2$, $E_{\vec\alpha_1}=\mathsf e$ and $E_{\vec\alpha_0}=\mathsf f$, and show that it becomes (-@eq-l6-lax) at imaginary coupling with $\vec H=\mathsf h/\sqrt2$ and $m=m_0/2$.
:::

::: {#exr-l6-backlund}
*(Redo.)* Show that the curvature of $\mathcal A'=G^{-1}\mathcal AG+G^{-1}\partial G$ is $G^{-1}$ times the curvature of $\mathcal A$ times $G$. Then do the $\partial_-$ half of the proof of @thm-l6-gauge in full.
:::

::: {#exr-l6-identities}
*(Redo.)* Prove the identities (-@eq-l6-identities) and the two further ones of @sec-l6-frozen by moving every $\mathsf s$ to the right. Derive the order $\lambda^{-1}$ of (-@eq-l6-time) and the second column of (-@eq-l6-four). Then verify $[\Pi,\mathsf D_1\mathsf O_2]=-\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h\,\mathsf O_1\mathsf D_2$ by writing $\mathsf D_1\mathsf O_2$ in terms of $\mathsf e$, $\mathsf f$ and diagonal matrices, and solve the two equations for $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ in the proof of @thm-l6-sklyanin.
:::

::: {#exr-l6-types}
*(Rediscover.)* Show that $\mathcal A_\pm(-\Psi)=\mathsf s\,\mathcal A_\pm(\Psi)\,\mathsf s$, and deduce that $L_d^+=L_d(\Phi,-\Psi)\,\mathsf s$ glues the linear problems on the type-I$_+$ conditions. On the vacuum, $L_d^+=\mathsf s+\frac\sigma\lambda=\frac\sigma\lambda\big(1+\frac\lambda\sigma\mathsf s\big)$. Compare with the book's $\tilde L_{\rm I_+}$ for $h=2$ (see its [defect matrix](book:eq-defect-lax-matrix)), and explain why type I$_+$ is "linear in $\lambda$" where type I$_-$ is linear in $1/\lambda$. For $a_r^{(1)}$, use Lecture 5's $\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j=-2\vec\mu_{j+1}$ and $\mathsf E=1-\mathsf D$ to show that $\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec w=\psi_j+\psi_{j+1}-2\phi_{j+1}$, and hence that (-@eq-l6-ar-Ld) is the book's form.
:::

::: {#exr-l6-zero}
*(Redo.)* Do the expansion of @sec-l6-charges at $\lambda\to0$. Show that in the gauge $e^{-i\Phi\mathsf h/4}$ the window becomes $e^{i\Delta\mathsf h/2}+\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf s$, find $W_1=\frac{\partial_-\Phi}{2m_0}\mathsf y$, and show that the coefficient of $\lambda$ in $\ln\tau_d$ is $\frac{m_0\ell}2+\frac1\sigma-\frac1{4m_0}\big(\beta^2(E+P)+\mathcal B+P_d\big)$.
:::

::: {#exr-l6-norming}
*(Explore.)* Make the heuristic of @sec-l6-knows precise. A soliton of rapidity $\theta$ corresponds to a bound state of the linear problem at $\lambda=-e^{-\theta}$: a solution that decays at both ends of the line. In the original gauge, $a_x$ at the vacuum $2\pi$ is minus $a_x$ at the vacuum $0$, so the decaying solution is along $(1,1)$ at both ends. The ratio of its coefficients at the two ends is the norming constant, and it contains $Y$'s constant $c$. Track the bound state across the window with $L_d^{-1}$, using $L_d=1+\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf s$ at $(0,0)$ and $L_d=1-\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf s$ at $(2\pi,2\pi)$, and recover $Y\to zY$. Why does the argument fail at $\theta=\theta_d$?
:::

::: {#exr-l6-rmatrix}
*(Redo.)* Compute $\{a_x(\lambda_1;x)\overset\otimes,a_x(\lambda_2;y)\}$ from $\{\Phi(x),\Phi_t(y)\}=\beta^2\delta(x-y)$. Only the terms of $a_x$ with $\Phi_t$ and with $\mathsf s_{\pm\Phi}$ have nonzero brackets. Show that $r=\alpha\,\mathsf h\otimes\mathsf h+\gamma\,\Pi$ commutes with $\mathsf h\otimes1+1\otimes\mathsf h$, and solve for $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ to obtain (-@eq-l6-rmatrix). For the sign of $\{T,T\}$, take a lattice of spacing $\varepsilon$, with $T=e^{-\varepsilon a_x}$ for one site and $\{\Phi_n,\partial_t\Phi_n\}=\beta^2/\varepsilon$, and expand to first order in $\varepsilon$.
:::

::: {#exr-l6-spin3}
*(Explore.)* Show that $\partial_-\big[(\partial_+^2\Phi)^2-\frac14(\partial_+\Phi)^4\big]+\partial_+\big[m_0^2\cos\Phi\,(\partial_+\Phi)^2\big]=0$ on solutions, so that $q_-$ is a conserved density with the current $j_-=m_0^2\cos\Phi\,(\partial_+\Phi)^2-(\partial_+^2\Phi)^2+\frac14(\partial_+\Phi)^4$, $\partial_tq_-+\partial_xj_-=0$. With a window, $\frac d{dt}\int q_-=j_-(\Psi)-j_-(\Phi)$ at $x=0$. Express $\partial_+\Psi$ and $\partial_+^2\Psi$ at $x=0$ through the defect conditions, and show that $\frac1{8m_0^3}\big(j_-(\Psi)-j_-(\Phi)\big)=-\frac d{dt}\mathcal D_{-3}$. Then compute $\frac1{8m_0^3}\int q_-\,dx$ for a soliton at rest and find $-\frac23$. Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon found the window by asking that this charge survive [@bcz2004].
:::

::: {#exr-l6-chain}
*(Explore.)* Take $N$ windows, each with its own canonical pair $(\Phi_n,\Psi_n)$, $\{\Phi_n,\Psi_m\}=-\beta^2\delta_{nm}$, and form $M(\lambda)=L_d^{(1)}(\lambda)\cdots L_d^{(N)}(\lambda)$. Show that the traces $\operatorname{tr}M(\lambda)$ Poisson-commute for all $\lambda$. Expand $\operatorname{tr}M$ in powers of $\sigma/\lambda$ for $N=2$ and find the first two commuting quantities. What changes if one factor is replaced by its inverse?
:::

::: {#exr-l6-two}
*(Explore.)* Verify the refactorization of @sec-l6-two-windows for $\Phi_0=0$, where $\Phi_1$ and $\Phi_2$ are solitons and $\Phi_{12}$ is the two-soliton solution. Then place two windows, with $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, at $x=0$ and $x=a$, and show that their combined effect on a passing soliton is the product of the two delays. What does the refactorization say about exchanging the two windows?
:::

## Where this comes from {#sec-l6-sources}

Lax introduced the representation of a nonlinear evolution equation as the compatibility of two linear problems [@lax1968], and Ablowitz, Kaup, Newell and Segur gave the $2\times2$ linear problem of the sine-Gordon equation and solved it by inverse scattering [@akns1973]. The Hamiltonian theory, with the classical r-matrix and the quadratic bracket of the transport matrix, is in the book of Faddeev and Takhtajan [@faddeev_takhtajan1987]. The relation between Bäcklund transformations and gauge (Darboux) transformations of the linear problem is classical [@rogers_schief2002]. Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon constructed the Lax pair of the window from two overlapping Lax pairs and found its defect matrix [@bcz2004; @bcz2004b]; in the affine Toda theories they found that the construction works only for $a_r^{(1)}$, and they expected that only one chirality of the higher charges survives each type [@bcz2004b], which the book shows is not so. Caudrelier built the generating function of all the modified charges with a defect matrix, described windows as Bäcklund transformations at a point and classified the defect matrices [@caudrelier2008]. Habibullin and Kundu derived the r-matrix structure on a lattice [@habibullin_kundu2008], Avan and Doikou from the r-matrix algebra [@avan_doikou2012a; @avan_doikou2012b], and Caudrelier and Kundu, and Caudrelier, in a second Poisson bracket in which the window is a canonical transformation [@caudrelier_kundu2015; @caudrelier2015]. Several things are our presentation, and we do not claim that they are new: the calculation with the matrices $\mathsf D$, $\mathsf O$, $\bar{\mathsf O}$ and the pairing argument of @thm-l6-frozen; the delay and the transmission factor as ratios of the eigenvalues of $L_d$; the closed forms (-@eq-l6-D3) and the stored spin-3 charge; the hand proof that the window determines the r-matrix; the refactorization of @sec-l6-two-windows; and the component form (-@eq-l6-ar-Ld). The book states the results in its sections on [Lax pairs with a defect](book:sec-defect-lax) and on [the defect monodromy and the classical r-matrix](book:sec-defect-r-matrix), and in its propositions on [the defect Lax matrix](book:prp-defect-lax), [the spin-two charges](book:prp-spin-two) and [the Poisson algebra of the defect matrix](book:prp-defect-involution).
